paragraphs.text: In the early 1990s, scientists at the US-based agricultural firm Cargill achieved a technological breakthrough when they succeeded in converting corn, a natural, renewable resource, into a polymer (or plastic) suitable for a broad variety of applications.

Once the initial technique had been developed, the company needed a partner with polymerization capabilities and access to plastics markets, and therefore formed a joint venture with the Dow Chemical Company, creating Cargill Dow Limited Liability Company (Cargill Dow LLC).
Cargill Dow now produces PLA, the world's first commercially available plastic made from an annually renewable resource such as corn. There are two main types of product:
NatureWorks™ PLA is a family of polymers (carbon-based molecules) made from non-petroleum based resources, which are used for packaging.
Ingeo is a family of polymers made in a similar manner to the packaging polymers. They are used to make fibers for textile production.

By applying their unique technology to the processing of natural plant products, Cargill Dow has created a more environmentally-friendly material that reaches the consumer in packaging, clothes and other products.

In nature, plants such as corn produce nutrients from carbon dioxide and water in the process of photosynthesis. The production of PLA begins when the corn is milled, separating the starch found in the grains of corn from the rest of the raw material. Unrefined dextrose (a type of sugar) is then processed from the starch and this is turned into lactic acid by fermentation. This is the same lactic acid that is used as a food additive and is found in muscle tissue in the human body. From this, a lactide is formed through condensation; this is then purified through vacuum distillation and finally, through a solvent-free melt process, it becomes a polymer, which is then used as the base for both NatureWorks™ PLA and for Ingeo.

Cargill Dow manufactures PLA at its plant in Nebraska, USA. This world-scale production facility allows the company to meet the rapidly growing international demand for the product. The plant has also provided a new market for producers of agricultural crops. Its location has proved to be a perfect fit based on a number of factors, including its proximity to existing milling operations, access to transportation, and the available labor force.

Cargill Dow uses Number 2 Yellow Dent corn, the most common corn variety, with more than 80% of the crop grown to feed animals. Number 2 Yellow Dent corn can also be used to make products like dextrose and fructose (used as sweeteners) and is considered safe as a raw material for human consumption. Cargill Dow's products are free of genetically modified material, and in fact do not require any such material during their production.

PLA is now actively competing with traditional materials in packaging and fiber applications throughout the world. Since PLA polymers are more grease-resistant and provide a better flavor and aroma barrier than existing petroleum-based polymers, grocery retailers are increasingly using this packaging for their fresh foods. As companies begin to explore this family of polymers, more potential applications are being identified. For example, they possess two properties that are particularly useful for drape fabrics and window furnishings. Their resistance to ultraviolet light is particularly appealing as this reduces the amount of fading in such fabrics, and their refractive index is low, which means fabrics constructed from these polymers can be made in deep colors without requiring large amounts of dye. In addition, sportswear-makers have been drawn to the product, as it has an inherent ability to absorb sweat from the surface of the body and, when blended with cotton and wool, the result is garments that are lighter and more comfortable.

PLA combines inexpensive large-scale fermentation with chemical processing to produce a value-added polymer product that improves the environment as well. As an alternative to traditional petroleum-based polymers, the production of PLA also uses 20% – 50% less fossil fuel, and releases lower amounts of greenhouse gases than comparable petroleum-based plastic; carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is absorbed when the feedstock is grown and is returned to the earth when the polymer is degraded.

Because the company is using raw materials that can be regenerated year after year, it is both cost-competitive and environmentally responsible. The technology has received many awards, including the Discover Award for Environmental Innovation, and has been allocated funding by the US Department of Energy for continued research and development into the utilization of renewable resources.
